newsitem.title: USA: TWA faces short-term pressure on profits.
newsitem.headline: TWA faces short-term pressure on profits.

text.p: Trans World Airlines, striving to win passengers following repeated bankrutpcies, faces new short-term pressure on profits after the crash of its Flight 800 off the coast of Long Island two months ago.
"They had expected to grow capacity 13 percent this quarter. But the loss of the aircraft affected that," said Brian Harris, an analyst with Lehman Brothers.
"With capacity down, and costs not going down, that would affect profitability," Harris said. Harris declined to predict the extent that TWA will fall short of its growth goals.

The July 17 crash of TWA's Paris-bound Boeing 747, which killed 230 people, has not siginficantly deterred travelers from TWA, analysts said. But it has prevented TWA from carrying out plans to boost profits with more flights.

Analysts said TWA benefitted from traffic increases during the peak summer travel period, reporting load factor gains in July and August despite the crash. Those gains have somewhat offset new security-related costs, they said.
"They're still moving in the right direction. They're the last fixer-upper in the industry," said Harris.
"The question is whether they are moving fast enough as they need to to get the job done before the next downturn in the industry," Harris said.
TWA still faces other obstacles. After the crash, it postponed a secondary equity offering that would have pumped about $159 million into the company.

Analysts said the St. Louis-based carrier also must stabilize its highly seasonal business and replace one of the oldest fleets among U.S. carriers -- with an average age of about 18.6 years, compared to an industry average of 11.9 years.
On Tuesday, TWA said its board approved the acquisition of 10 new McDonnell Douglas Corp MD83 aircraft.
The carrier's aircraft replacement efforts will keep its balance sheet highly leveraged for the next five years, analysts said.
Brokerage firm Goldman Sachs started coverage Tuesday of Trans World Airlines as "market underperform."
The total financial impact of the crash on TWA remains unknown, as investigators still search for the cause of the explosion and the bodies of 17 victims still missing.
The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board sought help from TWA for $5 million to help defray investigation costs that amount to more than $100,000 a day.
The NTSB also requested funds from Boeing Co, which made the downed 747 jetliner, and United Technologies' Pratt & Whitney Canada Inc unit, which made the jet's engine.
TWA said Tuesday it is still evaluating that request and has not paid any money for the NTSB's investigation. The carrier also has declined to comment on the financial impact of the crash.
